passages.t: Hezekiah's tears, and fifteen more years
passages.happening:
‘In those days Hezekiah became mortally ill’ (verse 1). Isaiah comes to him with the LORD's word: put your house in order, for you will die and not recover. Hezekiah turns his face to the wall and prays, “Please, O LORD, remember how I have walked before You faithfully and with wholehearted devotion; I have done what was good in Your sight” (verse 3). ‘And Hezekiah wept bitterly’ (verse 3).

Before Isaiah has left the middle courtyard, the word of the LORD comes to him. He is to go back and tell Hezekiah, ‘I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. I will surely heal you’ (verse 5). On the third day he will go up to the house of the LORD. The LORD will add fifteen years to his life and defend the city from the king of Assyria, for his own sake and for David's (verse 6). Isaiah has them put a poultice of figs on the boil, and Hezekiah recovers (verse 7).

Hezekiah asks for a sign. Isaiah offers him the shadow going forward ten steps or back ten. Going forward is easy, Hezekiah says; let it go back (verses 8-10). Isaiah calls to the LORD, ‘and He brought the shadow back the ten steps it had descended on the stairway of Ahaz’ (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
The phrase in those days places these events loosely, and they are probably told out of order. The promise to save the city from Assyria suggests that the illness came before or during the crisis of 701 BC. Hezekiah reigned twenty-nine years, and fifteen added years fit an illness around 702 or 701 BC and his death around 686 BC.

To put one's house in order meant to settle family and royal affairs, including the succession, before death. A poultice of figs was a known remedy for boils and skin infections, applied as a hot plaster. The text sets the remedy and the miracle side by side without any tension: God heals, and a remedy is used. The verb for heal, rapha, is the one in the LORD's name at Marah, the LORD who heals.

The stairway of Ahaz was apparently a set of steps on which the sun's shadow moved through the day, working as a kind of clock. Whether it was built for that is not known. Hezekiah asks for a sign, as his father Ahaz had refused to do. The verb see links this chapter's two scenes: the LORD has seen Hezekiah's tears, and soon the Babylonians will see everything in his palace.
passages.later: A psalm prays, ‘all night I flood my bed with weeping and drench my couch with tears’ (Psalm 6:6). When Nineveh turned from its evil ways, God ‘relented from the disaster He had threatened to bring upon them’ (Jonah 3:10).
passages.hard:
Did God change his mind about Hezekiah's death?

Isaiah first says that Hezekiah will not recover, and then, after the king's prayer, brings a promise of fifteen more years. Some readers take this as God truly responding to prayer in a way that changes the outcome, as the Bible often describes. Others stress that God's announcements of judgment are often conditional even when the condition is not stated, as with Jonah's message to Nineveh; the warning was meant to lead to a response. Both views agree that prayer is not a formality, and that God's purposes include the prayers of his people.

The story is not a promise that every prayer for healing will be answered with healing. Many faithful people have prayed and wept as Hezekiah did and were not healed, and the Bible does not say they prayed wrongly.

It needs to be said plainly. The Bible does not teach that sickness comes from too little faith, or that a person who stays ill did not believe enough. Paul prayed and was not healed, and no one blames him. If you live with chronic illness, pain or disability, you are not a failure of faith. Your worth to God does not rise or fall with your body. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a doctor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and wept, and God said he had seen his tears. Ask what that suggests about how God receives honest grief. And ask what you would do with fifteen more years.

passages.happening:
Merodach-baladan king of Babylon sends letters and a gift to Hezekiah, having heard of his illness (verse 12). Hezekiah welcomes the envoys and shows them everything: the silver, the gold, the spices, the precious oil, his armory and all his storehouses. ‘There was nothing in his palace or in all his dominion that Hezekiah did not show them’ (verse 13).

Isaiah comes and asks where the men came from and what they said. ‘They came from a distant land’, Hezekiah answers, ‘from Babylon’ (verse 14). What have they seen? “They have seen everything in my palace” (verse 15). Isaiah gives the LORD's word: the time will come when everything in the palace, everything his fathers stored up, ‘will be carried off to Babylon. Nothing will be left, says the LORD’ (verse 17). Some of his own descendants will be taken to serve in the palace of the king of Babylon (verse 18).

Hezekiah answers, “The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good” (verse 19). He thinks, “Will there not at least be peace and security in my lifetime?” (verse 19). The narrator closes his reign with the pool and the tunnel he built to bring water into the city, and his son Manasseh reigns (verses 20-21).
passages.hearers:
Merodach-baladan, Marduk-apla-iddina in Babylonian sources, was a Chaldean leader who seized Babylon's throne and held it against Assyria from about 721 to 710 BC, and briefly again around 703 BC, before Sennacherib drove him out. His embassy was almost certainly more than a get-well visit. He was looking for allies in the west against Assyria, which helps explain why Hezekiah showed off his treasury and armory. Showing wealth to foreign envoys was a way of presenting oneself as a desirable ally.

The chapter quietly turns the book's attention from Assyria to Babylon. Assyria has just been humbled. Babylon, still a small kingdom in revolt against Assyria, is named for the first time as the power that will one day empty Jerusalem, and Isaiah's words hang over every chapter until they come true. Isaiah's questions are like a prosecutor's, and Hezekiah answers with a kind of naive pride. The word in verse 18, saris, could mean a royal official in general, but in a foreign palace it often meant a man castrated to serve there. The prediction is often linked with the young men of Judah's royal family at the Babylonian court in Daniel, though Kings does not name them.

Hezekiah's tunnel, cut through rock beneath the City of David to bring water from the Gihon spring to the pool of Siloam inside the walls, still exists. An inscription found in it in 1880 describes the moment when the two crews digging from opposite ends met. Manasseh was twelve when he became king, so on the usual reckoning he was born in the added years.
passages.later: Chronicles says, ‘It was Hezekiah who blocked the upper outlet of the Spring of Gihon and channeled it down to the west side of the City of David’ (2 Chronicles 32:30). Daniel tells of young men taken ‘from the royal family and the nobility’ (Daniel 1:3) to serve in Babylon.
passages.hard:
Was Hezekiah's answer to Isaiah selfish?

His words in verse 19 are debated. Many readers find them self-centered: he is relieved that the disaster will come after his lifetime. Others read them as humble acceptance of God's word as just, with the thought of peace in his own days as relief that the judgment was put off. The narrator gives both his spoken words and his private thought, and leaves the reader to weigh them. What is clear is that the best king since David could still be flattered by a distant power, and could still think more of his own days than of his children's.
passages.asks: Hezekiah showed the Babylonians everything he had. Ask when you are tempted to win the admiration of powerful people by displaying what you have. And ask what responsibility you carry for those who will come after you.
